blocks.text: Say you have a column full of timestamps, order_date, signup_date, event_time, whatever it is. It is already proper datetime64 dtype, you converted it with pd.to_datetime() back in the changing data types lesson. Now what? Handing that raw column straight to a model does almost nothing useful. This lesson is about the dt accessor, the tool that lets you crack a datetime column open and pull out the pieces a model can actually learn from.

blocks.alt: A raw datetime column feeding a model directly compared to the dt accessor extracting day of week, month and hour as separate useful features
blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture: raw timestamps in, useful features out.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Think about what a raw datetime value actually is under the hood. pd.to_datetime() gives you a real Timestamp object, but under the hood pandas is storing it as a plain integer, nanoseconds since a fixed reference point back in 1970. If you hand that integer straight to a model as a single feature, you are asking it to find a relationship between a nine digit number and whatever you are trying to predict. That basically never works well.

code.content:
df["order_date"].astype("int64")
# 1751500800000000000
# a huge, mostly meaningless number to a model

blocks.text: But the individual pieces that timestamp is made of, the day of the week, the month, whether it falls on a weekend, are a completely different story. A model can absolutely learn that weekend orders behave differently from weekday orders, or that December looks nothing like a normal month for a retail business. Turning one raw timestamp into several separate, meaningful features is the entire point of this lesson. That reframing, from a single number the model cannot use to several numbers it very much can, is what feature engineering on a datetime column really means.
2. The dt Accessor

If a column has already been converted to datetime64 dtype, pandas gives you a special namespace attached to it called dt. You have already met its cousin. The str accessor from the string operations lesson let you run one vectorized operation, like str.lower() or str.contains(), across an entire column of text at once, no loop required. dt works exactly the same way, except every operation it exposes is about extracting or manipulating a piece of a date instead of a piece of text.

blocks.alt: The str accessor running vectorized text operations across a column next to the dt accessor running vectorized date operations across a column
blocks.caption: Same vectorized, elementwise idea, applied to dates instead of text.

blocks.text: The syntax is always the same shape: df[column].dt.attribute for a plain read on the value, or df[column].dt.method() when it needs parentheses because it is a method rather than a property. Both return a new Series, the same length as the original column, computed elementwise across every row in one vectorized pass.

Treat dt exactly the way you already treat str: reach for it instead of writing a python loop or an apply with a lambda. df["order_date"].dt.year runs across the whole column in one vectorized pass and will be dramatically faster than looping row by row once your DataFrame has any real size to it.

blocks.title: dt Needs a Real Datetime64 Column First
blocks.content: If the column is still object dtype, plain text that merely looks like a date, calling dt on it raises an AttributeError. Convert it first with pd.to_datetime(), covered in the changing data types lesson, before reaching for anything in this lesson.

blocks.text: 3. Extracting Basic Date Components
Once a column is datetime64, dt exposes a whole set of components you can pull straight out of it. These are the building blocks almost every datetime feature engineering pipeline starts with.

items: dt.day, the day of the month, 1 through 31
dt.hour, 0 through 23, only meaningful if the column actually carries a time component
dt.minute and dt.second, finer grained time components

blocks.text: 3.1 Year, Month and Day
These three are the ones you will reach for constantly. Each call returns an integer Series, same length as the original column.

code.content:
df["order_year"] = df["order_date"].dt.year
df["order_month"] = df["order_date"].dt.month
df["order_day"] = df["order_date"].dt.day

blocks.alt: A datetime column branching into dt.year, dt.month, dt.day and dt.hour as four separate extracted components
blocks.caption: Four separate features pulled out of one column, no loop involved.

blocks.text: 3.2 Hour and Minute

If the original column has a real time component attached, not just midnight for every row, dt.hour is genuinely useful. Website traffic, support ticket volume, and app usage all vary enormously by hour of day, and that is a strong feature for plenty of models.

Watch out for one thing here. If your source data was only ever a date with no time attached, pandas fills in midnight, 00:00:00, as the time for every row when it parses it. dt.hour will then return 0 for every single row, which is not useful information, it is just a side effect of how the column was created.

blocks.title: Check What Time Resolution Your Column Actually Has
blocks.content: Before you build features off dt.hour or dt.minute, check whether the source data genuinely varies at that resolution. A column parsed from a plain date column will report hour 0 for every row, and a feature that is the same value for every row is worthless to a model.

blocks.text: 4. Day of Week as an Integer and as a Name
dt.dayofweek is one of the single most useful datetime features you can engineer, and pandas gives you two ways to get at it.
This returns a plain integer, 0 through 6, where Monday is 0 and Sunday is 6. It is compact, it sorts predictably, and most models are perfectly happy consuming it directly as a number.

dt.day_name() gives you the same information as an actual readable string, Monday, Tuesday, and so on. It is not something you feed to most models directly, but it is exactly what you want for a chart label, a print statement while you are debugging, or a groupby result you want to read at a glance.

blocks.alt: dt.dayofweek returning a plain integer from 0 through 6 next to dt.day_name returning a readable string like Monday
blocks.caption: Same information, two different shapes for two different jobs.

blocks.text: 5. Engineering the is_weekend Feature

dt.dayofweek is genuinely important on its own, but one specific feature built from it comes up constantly in real projects: is_weekend. Since Saturday is 5 and Sunday is 6, checking whether dayofweek is 5 or 6 tells you whether a given row fell on a weekend.

blocks.alt: dt.dayofweek being checked against 5 or 6 to produce a true or false is_weekend feature
blocks.caption: One comparison turns a weekly cycle into a clean yes or no feature.

blocks.text: This single boolean feature often carries more predictive power than you would expect. Retail sales, restaurant traffic, ride share demand, gym check ins, all of them shift meaningfully between weekday and weekend behavior, and a model that can see is_weekend directly does not have to reconstruct that pattern indirectly from the raw date.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Feature given to the model","What the model can learn"],"rows":[["Raw order_date timestamp","Almost nothing directly, the number itself carries no learnable weekly pattern"],["day_of_week integer","Which of the seven weekly patterns a row belongs to"],["is_weekend boolean","The single sharpest weekday versus weekend split, often the strongest signal of the three"]]}

blocks.title: Day of Week Frequently Beats the Raw Date
blocks.content: For problems like sales forecasting or traffic prediction, day_of_week and is_weekend are often far more predictive than the literal calendar date. The date tells the model almost nothing about repeating weekly behavior on its own, the day of week tells it exactly that.

blocks.text: 6. Extracting Quarter for Business Data
Plenty of business and financial data is organized around quarters rather than months. dt.quarter gives you that grouping directly, an integer from 1 to 4.

blocks.alt: dt.quarter splitting a datetime column into four business quarters, Q1 through Q4
blocks.caption: A coarser, calendar aware grouping business and finance data is usually organized around anyway.

blocks.text: This is a natural feature whenever you are working with revenue, earnings, budget cycles, or anything else a business actually plans around a quarterly rhythm. It is a coarser, sometimes more stable, signal than month when a full twelve way split would be too granular for how much data you have.

blocks.text: 7. Computing Durations Between Two Dates

A single datetime column gets you components. Two datetime columns get you something arguably even more useful: a duration between them. Customer tenure, delivery time, time to resolution, all of these are duration features built by subtracting one datetime column from another.
7.1 Subtracting Datetime Columns
Subtract one datetime Series from another and pandas does not give you back a number, it gives you back a Timedelta, a proper representation of an elapsed span of time.

code.content:
delivery_time = df["delivered_date"] - df["order_date"]
delivery_time
# 0   5 days 03:12:00
# 1   2 days 00:41:00
# dtype: timedelta64[ns]

blocks.alt: Two datetime columns, delivered_date and order_date, being subtracted to produce a Timedelta result
blocks.caption: Subtracting two datetimes never gives you a plain number, it gives you a Timedelta.

blocks.text: That Timedelta carries days, hours, minutes and seconds all bundled together, which is exact and correct, but it is not yet the kind of plain numeric feature most models want to consume.
7.2 Pulling a Plain Integer With dt.days

This is where dt shows up again, this time on a Timedelta Series rather than a datetime Series. dt.days extracts just the whole number of days out of that duration, discarding the leftover hours and minutes, and hands you back a plain integer.

blocks.alt: dt.days pulling a plain integer number of days out of a Timedelta to create a delivery_days feature
blocks.caption: The Timedelta collapses down to one clean integer column.

blocks.text: This exact pattern, subtract two datetime columns then call dt.days on the result, is one of the most common feature engineering moves you will make. Customer tenure is today minus signup_date. Delivery time is delivered_date minus order_date. Time to resolution is closed_at minus opened_at. Same two lines, different column names, every time.
8. The Cyclical Feature Gotcha

Here is a genuinely important trap that catches people who are new to this. Month and day of week look like ordinary integers, but they are not ordinary integers, they are cyclical. December is month 12 and January is month 1. Numerically those two values are about as far apart as they can possibly be. In real calendar time, they are neighbors, December 31st is followed immediately by January 1st.

blocks.alt: December as month 12 and January as month 1 sitting far apart numerically while actually being adjacent days in real time
blocks.caption: The gap between 12 and 1 is huge on a number line and nonexistent on a calendar.

blocks.title: A Plain Integer Does Not Know About the Wraparound
blocks.content: If you feed month straight into a model as the integer 1 through 12, the model has no way to know that 12 and 1 are actually next to each other. It will treat December and January as maximally different, when in reality they are adjacent. The exact same problem hits day_of_week, Sunday, 6, and Monday, 0, are adjacent days in reality but sit at opposite ends of the integer range.

blocks.text: For plenty of models this does not matter much, tree based models like random forests and gradient boosting can often work around it by splitting on the value directly. But for models that are sensitive to numeric distance, like linear models, k nearest neighbors, or neural networks, the gap can genuinely hurt.
8.1 Sine and Cosine Encoding as the Fix

The standard fix is to encode the cyclical value as a point on a circle instead of a straight line, using sine and cosine together. December and January end up close together on that circle, exactly the way they are close together in real time. This lesson will not go deep into the math behind it, just flag that it is the standard, well known technique to reach for whenever a cyclical feature like month, day of week, or hour genuinely needs to respect its own wraparound.

code.content:
import numpy as np

df["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["order_date"].dt.month / 12)
df["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["order_date"].dt.month / 12)

blocks.alt: A plain month integer branching into sine of month and cosine of month, which combine into a cyclical encoding
blocks.caption: Two smooth columns replace one integer, and together they preserve the wraparound.

blocks.text: Two new columns replace the one raw month integer, and together they preserve the wraparound a plain integer throws away. Keep this technique in your back pocket. You will not need it for every project, but when a cyclical feature is clearly hurting a model's accuracy, this is where you reach.
9. Worked Example: Engineering Features From order_date

Put all of it together on a realistic table. Say you have an orders DataFrame with a raw order_date column and a delivered_date column, both already converted to datetime64 with pd.to_datetime(). Here is a full feature engineering pass across both.

code.content:
df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"])
df["delivered_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["delivered_date"])

df["order_day_of_week"] = df["order_date"].dt.dayofweek
df["is_weekend"] = df["order_date"].dt.dayofweek >= 5
df["order_quarter"] = df["order_date"].dt.quarter

delivery_time = df["delivered_date"] - df["order_date"]
df["delivery_days"] = delivery_time.dt.days

blocks.alt: A raw order_date column branching into day of week, is_weekend and quarter features, plus order_date and delivered_date together producing a delivery_days feature
blocks.caption: One raw column pair, four engineered features, zero loops.

blocks.content: {"headers":["New column","Built from","What it captures"],"rows":[["order_day_of_week","order_date.dt.dayofweek","Which day of the week the order was placed"],["is_weekend","order_date.dt.dayofweek","Whether the order landed on a Saturday or Sunday"],["order_quarter","order_date.dt.quarter","Which business quarter the order falls in"],["delivery_days","delivered_date minus order_date, then dt.days","How many days the delivery actually took"]]}

blocks.text: One raw column plus one paired column just became four genuinely useful features, none of which needed a single explicit loop. That is the whole value of the dt accessor: it takes something a model cannot use directly and turns it into several things it can.
10. Recap and What Is Next

items: A raw datetime column is close to useless to a model on its own, it is really just a large number under the hood.
The dt accessor is the datetime equivalent of str, one vectorized call extracts a component from every row at once.
dt.year, dt.month, dt.day and dt.hour pull the basic building blocks out of a datetime column.
dt.dayofweek returns an integer, 0 through 6 for Monday through Sunday, and dt.day_name() returns the same thing as a readable string.
is_weekend, built by checking whether dayofweek is 5 or 6, is one of the most consistently useful features you can derive from a date.
dt.quarter groups dates into the four periods most business and financial reporting is organized around.
Subtracting two datetime columns produces a Timedelta, and calling dt.days on that Timedelta pulls out a plain integer duration, the pattern behind features like tenure and delivery time.
Month and day of week are cyclical, not ordinary integers, and sine and cosine encoding is the standard fix when that wraparound actually matters to your model.

blocks.text: This lesson deliberately stayed at the feature engineering level, pulling useful signals out of a column that is already datetime64 dtype. There is a lot more to pandas datetime handling than this: the Timestamp object itself, date_range for generating date sequences, and resampling for aggregating time indexed data are all coming up in the dedicated Time Series with Pandas module later in this course, which goes into that mechanics in real depth. For now, you have what you need to turn any datetime column into features a model can actually learn from.
